concepts.name: Authentication versus authorization
concepts.summary: Explain that authentication verifies who a user is while authorization decides what that verified user may do.

concepts.name: Why passwords are hashed
concepts.summary: Explain why a server stores a one-way hash of a password rather than the password itself.

concepts.name: Credentials and authentication factors
concepts.summary: Recall that credentials such as passwords, devices and biometrics are grouped into knowledge, possession and inherence factors.

concepts.name: Session as login memory
concepts.summary: Understand that because HTTP is stateless, a server issues an identifier after login so later requests are recognised as the same user.

concepts.name: Cookies carrying session identifiers
concepts.summary: Recall that a browser stores a session identifier in a cookie and sends it automatically with each request to that site.

concepts.name: Least privilege principle
concepts.summary: Explain why users and processes should receive only the permissions they need.

concepts.name: Multi-factor authentication purpose
concepts.summary: Understand that requiring a second independent factor limits damage when a password is stolen.

misconceptions.text: Authentication and authorization are two names for the same thing.
Encrypting passwords and hashing them are the same, and a site should be able to show you your original password.
Once a user is logged in, the server automatically knows who they are on every request without any identifier being sent.

concepts.name: Salted password hashing
concepts.summary: Apply a unique random salt per password so identical passwords produce different hashes and precomputed tables fail.

concepts.name: Slow adaptive hash functions
concepts.summary: Choose a deliberately slow, tunable password hashing function instead of a fast general-purpose hash.

concepts.name: Login flow implementation
concepts.summary: Implement a login endpoint that verifies a hash, creates a session and returns uniform error messages.

concepts.name: Secure cookie attributes
concepts.summary: Set HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite on session cookies and explain the threat each one reduces.

concepts.name: Session lifecycle management
concepts.summary: Create, expire and destroy sessions on the server so logout and timeouts truly end access.

concepts.name: Role-based access control basics
concepts.summary: Understand how assigning users to roles that bundle permissions simplifies access decisions.

concepts.name: Server-side permission checks
concepts.summary: Apply an authorization check on the server for every protected request rather than relying on hidden interface elements.

misconceptions.text: Hashing passwords with SHA-256 is as good as bcrypt because both are secure hashes.
A salt must be kept secret to be effective.
Hiding a button or menu link from unauthorised users is enough to protect a feature.

concepts.name: Session fixation and hijacking defenses
concepts.summary: Analyse how session identifiers are stolen or imposed and apply regeneration on login, entropy and transport protection.

concepts.name: CSRF protection mechanisms
concepts.summary: Analyse why cookie-based authentication enables cross-site request forgery and choose tokens or SameSite policies to counter it.

concepts.name: Token-based authentication with JWT
concepts.summary: Apply signed tokens carrying claims, validating signature, algorithm, expiry and audience on each request.

concepts.name: Access and refresh token tradeoffs
concepts.summary: Compare stateless tokens with server sessions, including revocation difficulty and the use of short-lived access with refresh tokens.

concepts.name: OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow
concepts.summary: Apply the authorization code flow with PKCE, identifying the resource owner, client, authorization server and resource server.

concepts.name: OpenID Connect for login
concepts.summary: Distinguish OAuth authorization from OpenID Connect authentication and validate an ID token for sign-in.

concepts.name: Broken access control analysis
concepts.summary: Analyse code for missing ownership and role checks that allow users to reach other users' resources.

concepts.name: Brute force and credential stuffing defense
concepts.summary: Analyse automated guessing attacks and weigh rate limiting, lockout and breached-password checks as defenses.

misconceptions.text: A JWT is encrypted, so its contents are hidden from anyone who holds it.
OAuth 2.0 is an authentication protocol that proves who the user is.
Storing a JWT in local storage is safer than a cookie because CSRF no longer applies, with no other risk.

concepts.name: Attribute-based and policy-based access
concepts.summary: Analyse when role models become too coarse and policies using user, resource and context attributes fit better.

concepts.name: Centralised authorization architecture
concepts.summary: Evaluate designs that separate policy decision from enforcement and keep checks consistent across services.

concepts.name: Token validation and key management
concepts.summary: Evaluate token verification practices, including key rotation, algorithm pinning and defenses against forged tokens.

concepts.name: Token revocation and lifetime strategy
concepts.summary: Evaluate revocation approaches such as introspection, denylists and short lifetimes against latency and risk requirements.

concepts.name: Passwordless and phishing-resistant authentication
concepts.summary: Analyse how public-key credentials bound to an origin resist phishing compared with passwords and one-time codes.

concepts.name: Federated identity and SSO design
concepts.summary: Evaluate single sign-on designs, trust relationships and account-linking risks across identity providers.

concepts.name: Account recovery threat modelling
concepts.summary: Analyse reset and recovery flows as alternate authentication paths and identify weaknesses such as guessable or reusable links.

concepts.name: Service-to-service authentication
concepts.summary: Evaluate mechanisms for authenticating workloads, such as client credentials and mutual TLS, with scoped permissions.

misconceptions.text: Adding more roles always scales access control cleanly as an application grows.
Any valid signature on a token means the token is acceptable for this service.
SMS one-time codes are as phishing-resistant as WebAuthn.

concepts.name: Zero trust access architecture
concepts.summary: Evaluate architectures that authenticate and authorize every request using identity, device and context rather than network position.

concepts.name: Authorization model design
concepts.summary: Design a scalable authorization model, choosing between role, attribute and relationship-based approaches for a product's sharing needs.

concepts.name: Identity protocol vulnerability assessment
concepts.summary: Assess an OAuth, OIDC or SAML deployment for flaws such as open redirects, missing state checks and token replay.

concepts.name: Sender-constrained tokens
concepts.summary: Evaluate binding tokens to a client key so that a stolen token cannot be replayed by another party.

concepts.name: Adaptive and risk-based authentication
concepts.summary: Design policies that raise authentication requirements based on risk signals while managing friction and false positives.

concepts.name: Multi-tenant identity architecture
concepts.summary: Design identity and authorization for multi-tenant systems that isolate tenants, delegate administration and support enterprise federation.

concepts.name: Authentication migration and incident response
concepts.summary: Plan migrations such as password hash upgrades or IdP changes and responses to credential or signing key compromise.

concepts.name: Authorization testing and auditing
concepts.summary: Evaluate test strategies, audit logs and policy analysis that verify access rules hold across a system.

misconceptions.text: Placing services in a private network removes the need for per-request authentication and authorization.
One authorization model such as RBAC fits every product without modification.
Using a standard protocol like OAuth makes a deployment secure regardless of how it is configured.
